974.title: Sudama's handful of rice
974.hook: a poor friend brings Krishna a bundle of flattened rice, and Krishna eats it gladly
974.carry: offered with love, a leaf is enough for god
974.howItsDone: In home and temple puja, Hindus offer simple things such as flowers, fruit, water and tulsi leaves before the deity, and the story of Sudama's flattened rice is widely retold to show that what God wants is the love behind the gift.

segments.voice: A poor brahmin stands at the gates of Krishna's palace in Dvaraka. Tradition calls him Sudama. He and Krishna studied with the same teacher as boys. Now he's thin, his cloth is worn, and his wife has sent him with the only gift the house could find: a few handfuls of flattened rice, tied in a rag. Inside, everything shines. He's too ashamed to hand it over. And Krishna, hugging his old friend, asks: what did you bring me?
screen: `SUDAMA AT THE PALACE GATE.` → `A BUNDLE OF FLATTENED RICE.` → `WHAT DID YOU BRING ME?`

segments.voice: This is from the Bhagavata Purana. Before Sudama can answer, Krishna says the line he once spoke to Arjuna in the Gita, chapter nine, in paraphrase: whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, I accept that offering of love. Then he pulls the bundle out of his friend's hands and eats a handful of the rice, gladly, and reaches for another, until Queen Rukmini gently stops his hand. Sudama walks home without having asked for a thing, and finds his hut has become a palace. That's the teaching under every puja, the worship at a home shrine or a temple. The tray holds a banana, a few marigolds, a tulsi leaf, a little water. Nothing on it is expensive, and that's the point: God isn't being paid. God is being loved. The verse asks for bhakti, devotion, the love behind the hand. Then the Gita's next verse widens the tray to hold the whole day: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, whatever discipline you take on, do it as an offering to me. So puja doesn't end at the shrine. This week we sketched a year of service. On this reading, all of it can go on the tray, small and loved, like a handful of rice. Tomorrow, the same Krishna, not in a palace but in a dark forest, walked home by someone who loves him.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `KRISHNA EATS THE RICE.` · `GOD ISN'T PAID. GOD IS LOVED.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, AN OFFERING.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE YEAR ON THE TRAY.`

segments.voice: If there's something small within reach, a leaf, a glass of water, a piece of fruit, hold it in your hands the way Sudama held his bundle; if not, just open them. Let the year of service you've sketched come to mind piece by piece, the reason, your own service, the gift, the guest, the rhythm, and set each one in your hands. If you pray, offer it to the one you pray to, the way families set a tulsi leaf or a flower before the home shrine; if not, rest with the weight of it, small and freely given.
Puja. Worship at the home shrine or the temple: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, given with love. Not a payment. A gift.

975.title: Walking God home
975.hook: the sky is dark with clouds, and Radha is told to take him home
975.carry: bhakti: the lord of all, close enough to love
975.tomorrow: Radha at the edge of the dance
975.howItsDone: The Gita Govinda has been sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri for centuries; its songs are sung in Hindu devotional settings and performed in classical music and Odissi dance, and the hymn to the avatars with its refrain jaya jagadisha hare is sung on its own as well.

segments.voice: The sky is heavy with clouds. The forest is dark with tamala trees. Night is coming on, and the boy is nervous. So Nanda, the cowherd chief, turns to Radha: take him home. That's how the Gita Govinda begins, with a walk home through the dark. And the verse hails what follows on the bank of the river Yamuna: the secret love of Radha and Madhava, one of Krishna's names. After our days on the Bhagavad Gita, the path turns from Krishna the teacher on a battlefield to Krishna the beloved in a forest.
screen: `CLOUDS, DARK TREES, NIGHT.` → `TAKE HIM HOME.` → `FROM BATTLEFIELD TO FOREST.`

segments.voice: Gita Govinda means the song of Govinda, the cowherd, another name for Krishna. It's a love poem, and it says so up front. A few lines in, Jayadeva gives an invitation. If your heart is moved by remembering Hari, and if you're curious about the arts of love, then listen to these sweet, soft, lovely words. Remembering God and the play of lovers, offered as one door. Then, before the love story starts, Jayadeva sings a hymn through the Lord's descents into the world, the avatars: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, and on through Rama and the Buddha to Kalki, one stanza each. Every stanza ends with the same refrain: jaya jagadisha hare, victory to you, Hari, Lord of the world. So the reader meets the cosmic Lord first, the one who saves worlds in many forms, and only then the nervous boy Radha is walking home under the clouds. Same Lord. That's one of bhakti's boldest teachings, named plainly: the God of the whole universe comes close enough to be loved like a person, a child to be walked home, a beloved. You don't have to shrink God to love God up close. For centuries the Gita Govinda has been sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and Odissi dancers still perform its songs. Jayadeva doesn't explain the paradox. He just sings it.
screen: `THE SONG OF GOVINDA, THE COWHERD.` · `A HYMN TO THE LORD'S DESCENTS.` · `THE COSMIC LORD, THEN THE BOY.` · `CLOSE ENOUGH TO LOVE.` · then, large: `JAYA JAGADISHA HARE.`

segments.voice: Hear the opening again: clouds, dark trees, night coming, and Radha asked to walk the boy home. Now let two pictures sit side by side: the Lord of the whole world, fish, tortoise, man-lion, and the boy under the clouds. If you pray, let the refrain move quietly with the breath, jaya jagadisha hare, the way it's still sung at home and in temples. If not, simply hold the two pictures together, something vast and someone near, and breathe.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda, it's love for the Lord of the world, close enough to walk home.

976.title: Radha at the edge of the dance
976.hook: spring arrives in the forest, and Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone but her
976.carry: viraha: longing for god is devotion too
976.howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotion, the Gita Govinda's songs of Radha's longing are sung and danced, and viraha, longing in separation, is honored as a mood of devotion in its own right.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the opening of the Gita Govinda: the Lord of all, praised in every descent, close enough to love and walk home.
screen: `BHAKTI.` · `TAKE HIM HOME.`

segments.voice: Clove vines curl in a soft southern breeze. Bees hum around the flowering trees. The cuckoo is calling. Jayadeva piles up the details of spring until the forest seems almost too sweet to stand in. Into it walks Radha, with a friend at her side, and the friend points. Look. There's Hari, playing in the spring woods, dancing with the young cowherd women. The song's refrain says this season is hard on anyone apart from the one they love. And Radha is standing at the edge of the dance, apart.
screen: `CLOVE VINES, BEES, THE CUCKOO.` → `LOOK: HARI IS DANCING.` → `RADHA, AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The friend keeps singing, in paraphrase. Here, in the lovely spring, Hari plays, dancing with the young women: a cruel season for those apart from love. She describes him, one woman after another drawing close, each sure she has his attention. And Radha, the poem says, goes away. Not to confront him. She slips off into a bower of vines, hurt and jealous, and sits by herself. She doesn't stop loving him. In her song, she remembers him: the flute, the playful glances, the way he looked at her. Even while she's angry, her mind keeps returning to Hari. She tells her friend that her heart won't let him go, though he's with the others. That's the bhakti the poem cares about. Devotion, in the Gita Govinda, isn't calm. It has jealousy in it, and hurt, and memory, and the stubborn turning of the heart back to the one it loves. Some Vaishnava traditions have a name for this longing in separation, viraha, and treat it as a doorway rather than a failure. Radha's ache at the edge of the dance becomes, for them, a picture of the soul when God seems to be everywhere except close. For a devotee whose God feels far, that's the teaching: the longing itself is devotion, not failure. The poem doesn't scold her or hurry to fix things. And somewhere in the forest, as we'll hear tomorrow, Krishna has noticed she's gone.
screen: `HARI DANCES IN THE SPRING WOODS.` · `RADHA SLIPS AWAY TO A BOWER.` · `SHE KEEPS REMEMBERING HIM.` · `VIRAHA: LONGING IN SEPARATION.` · then, large: `THE HEART TURNS BACK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time you stood at the edge of something, a party, a group, apart from the one you most wanted near, and let the memory be there without arguing, like Radha in the bower. Notice what the heart does, whether it turns away or keeps turning back. If you pray, you can bring that longing, as it is, to the one you pray to; if not, let spring keep blooming around the feeling.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In Radha's bower, it's viraha: longing that keeps turning back, even when it hurts.

977.howItsDone: Singers in Vaishnava communities perform the Gita Govinda's songs in temples and in concert, often one song at a time, and dancers in classical forms such as Odissi act out scenes like Krishna's lament by the river.

segments.voice: Krishna is sitting by the river Yamuna, alone, and he is not doing well. A little while ago he was at the center of a spring dance in the forest, everyone around him. Then he noticed someone missing. Radha had seen him there, surrounded, and had quietly gone. He left the dance and searched the thickets and the vine bowers. Nothing. Now he has sat down on the bank, and Jayadeva lets us listen while he talks to himself. It isn't the speech a listener might expect from a god.
screen: `A DANCE, AND SOMEONE MISSING.` → `HE SEARCHES THE THICKETS.` → `ALONE ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: Here is his song, in paraphrase. She saw me surrounded by the other women, and she walked away. I didn't stop her. I was afraid, because I knew I was in the wrong. Then the refrain, again and again: Hari, Hari, through my own carelessness she has gone, angry, it seems. What will she do now? What will she say to me, after I've been away so long? What good is wealth, or people, or a home, without her? He sees her face in his mind, the eyebrows drawn together in anger, and speaks to her as if she were there: forgive me, I won't do it again, let me see you. This is the Lord of the poem, the one the opening hymn praised in every one of his descents into the world. And here he sits, admitting a mistake. How do devotees hold this? In Vaishnava traditions, one answer is the word lila, play. The divine takes on a lover's part fully, faults and all, so that love can be shown in its whole range: delight, hurt, regret, longing. It's easy to picture bhakti running one way, the soul reaching up toward God. Here it runs the other way too. God is the one who misses, rehearsing an apology by the river. For a devotee, that changes prayer: you aren't only reaching for God; on this reading, God is already looking for you. And Jayadeva closes his songs by naming himself, offering what he has sung.
screen: `I DIDN'T STOP HER. I WAS AFRAID.` · `WHAT WILL SHE SAY TO ME?` · `LILA: LOVE IN ITS WHOLE RANGE.` · `GOD IS THE ONE WHO MISSES.` · then, large: `HARI, HARI, SHE HAS GONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've let walk away without a word: a friend you stopped calling, a small hurt you saw and didn't answer. Don't fix anything; just sit on the riverbank with it, the way Krishna does in the poem, and let yourself see their face. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if you don't, simply stay with the memory, and breathe.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda it runs both ways: today, the one who longs is Krishna.

segments.voice: Sandal paste on the skin. Moonlight through the leaves. A soft wind off the southern hills. In poems like this one, these are the comforts of a hot evening, the things that cool a body down. Now a friend of Radha's comes to Krishna, where he waits in the forest, with a report. Everything that ought to soothe her, she says, is burning her. This is Radha's side, carried by someone who has just been sitting with her.

segments.voice: Here's the friend's song, in paraphrase. She blames the sandal paste. She blames the rays of the moon. They don't cool her; they torment her. The breeze from the sandalwood hills feels to her like poison. Even a bed of flowers gives her no rest. And the refrain keeps returning: in separation from you, Krishna, she is miserable. That's viraha again: the moon is the same moon, but the one she loves isn't there, so every sweet thing points to him. Now notice who is singing. Not Radha. Not Krishna. Her friend, her sakhi. She doesn't argue Radha out of her grief, and she doesn't scold Krishna. She sits with one, walks to the other, and tells the truth about what she saw. In Chaitanya's tradition, this friend matters enormously. There, Radha is Krishna's own power of love, and devotees don't usually picture themselves as Radha at all. They take the place of her friends and helpers: the ones who carry messages, prepare the bower, and are happiest when the two meet. That's a teaching about the self. The devotee's joy isn't in being the center. It's in serving a love bigger than you: the love between Radha and Krishna. You can see it in temple life: the cooks who make food for the deity, the singers who lead kirtan so others can come close, the ones who arrange the flowers and are never seen. Read that way, the friend's report is a prayer, and her running feet are devotion.

segments.voice: Feel the cool air at the edge of the nostrils for a few breaths. Then bring to mind someone whose hurt you know, someone who can't easily say it themselves. Picture carrying their truth, gently and honestly, the way the sakhi carries Radha's to Krishna. If you pray, carry them into your prayer now, by name, asking nothing for yourself; if you don't, hold them in mind, and ask what one honest word on their behalf would sound like.
Bhakti. Devotion. In the friend's song, it's a love that runs on someone else's errand: the sakhi serving a love bigger than herself.

979.title: Go, Madhava, go
979.hook: Radha waits all night in the place they agreed on, and at dawn he finally turns up
979.carry: bhakti has room for honest anger at god
979.howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotional performance, Radha's mana, her loving anger, is a recognized mood: singers and Odissi or Bharatanatyam dancers perform her song of dismissal at dawn as part of the Gita Govinda's story of separation and reunion.

segments.voice: The plan was simple: meet in the bower by the river, tonight. Radha goes. She waits. The moon comes up over the forest, and he doesn't come. She hears a leaf move and thinks it's him. It isn't. The whole night goes by like that. Then, at dawn, there he is, walking up through the trees with the look of someone who hasn't slept. Before he can say a word, she knows where he's been. What does a devotee, in a poem about God, say to God at a moment like this? Jayadeva gives her the floor.
screen: `MEET IN THE BOWER TONIGHT.` → `THE MOON RISES. NO ONE.` → `AT DAWN, THERE HE IS.`

segments.voice: The poem lingers on what she sees, in paraphrase. His eyes are red from a night without sleep. There are marks on him, traces left by someone else. And her song has a refrain sharp enough to sting: go, Madhava, go, Keshava. Don't speak your deceiving words. Go to the one who kept you up all night. She doesn't soften it or pretend to be fine. And the poem doesn't correct her, not yet. It lets her anger stand on the page, in front of the one the poem calls Lord. Vaishnava poetics has a name for this loving anger: mana, the wounded pride of a lover who knows her worth. It's treated as one of love's real moods, not a fault to hide. Read, as some devotees read it, with Radha as the soul, the scene suggests that bhakti doesn't have to be polite. A devotee may come before God disappointed, even furious, and the relationship holds. That's the teaching, plainly: bhakti has room for honest anger at God. Many Hindus who pray know this: you can bring the hurt to the shrine as it is. In the poem it more than holds: Krishna won't stop seeking her. Later, her friend will gently tell her she's held on long enough. But first, the poem gives her this. An honest complaint is itself a way of staying in the room. Indifference would say nothing. Radha says everything.
screen: `RED EYES. MARKS. NO SLEEP.` · `GO, MADHAVA. GO, KESHAVA.` · `MANA: LOVE'S WOUNDED PRIDE.` · `THE COMPLAINT KEEPS HER IN THE ROOM.` · then, large: `DON'T SPEAK YOUR DECEIVING WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let the shoulders drop and bring to mind one disappointment you've been carrying quietly, with a person, with life, or with God, if God is part of your life. Don't argue it away or make it bigger; just name it to yourself, plainly, the way Radha does, and notice that you're still here, still facing it. If you pray, bring it into your prayer just as it is; if you don't, let it be said inside, and keep breathing.
Bhakti. Devotion. In the Gita Govinda it has room for mana, love's honest anger, which still keeps facing the beloved.

980.title: Radha goes to him
980.hook: Radha's friend says she's held on long enough, and Radha walks through the dark to Krishna
980.carry: smarana: bring the beloved back to mind
980.howItsDone: In bhakti traditions, smarana, remembering the deity, is practiced through repeating a divine name (often on a mala), singing, and hearing stories; Vaishnava devotees sing and dance the Gita Govinda's songs, and it has long been sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri.

segments.voice: Radha has sent him away. Now her friend sits with her in the bower and says it plainly: you've held on to your anger long enough. Then Krishna himself comes back and pleads with her, the Lord of the world asking his beloved to forgive him. And the friend says it once more: go. He's waiting in the grove by the river. So Radha goes, slowly, a little shy, through the dark trees. In the poem's last songs they're together at last, and she asks him to set her ornaments straight, and he does.
screen: `YOU'VE HELD ON LONG ENOUGH.` → `KRISHNA COMES BACK AND PLEADS.` → `RADHA GOES TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Look back over the week and one thing keeps happening: somebody is remembering somebody. Krishna by the river keeps seeing Radha's face. Radha can't look at the moon without thinking of him. At dawn, every sharp word she says is about him. Nobody in this poem forgets, and that's why they find each other again. Jayadeva named it before the story began: if your heart is moved by remembering Hari, listen. Remembering is smarana. In the Bhagavata, the boy Prahlada lists the ways of devotion, and among them are hearing about Vishnu, singing about him, and remembering him. There, remembering isn't something that happens to you. It's something you do: bring the beloved back to mind, again and again, in the middle of ordinary life. That's why Hindus repeat a divine name on a mala, sing kirtan, and tell the same stories every year though everyone knows the ending. And it's why the Gita Govinda has been sung in worship at Puri for centuries: singing it is remembering Hari. Every dancer who walks Radha to the grove is doing what the poem asked for in its first lines. Just before the Gita Govinda, Sudama's rice went on the tray. Smarana is an offering that needs no tray. The hands can be still while the mind brings the beloved back.
screen: `NOBODY IN THE POEM FORGETS.` · `PRAHLADA'S LIST: HEAR, SING, REMEMBER.` · `A NAME ON A MALA.` · `AN OFFERING THAT NEEDS NO TRAY.` · then, large: `SMARANA.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose a name you already use, Krishna, Rama, Shiva, the Mother, and let it rest in the mind with each breath, the way people count a name on a mala. If you don't, bring to mind the face of someone you love. When the mind drifts, notice where it went, and bring the name or the face back, gently. That return is the practice, the same one Radha and Krishna kept all week.
Bhakti. Devotion. This week the Gita Govinda showed it as the Lord close enough to love, longing on both sides, honest anger, and smarana, remembering the beloved again and again.
